name: Wendy Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, I'm 27, and I work at Hale & Co, a family accounting firm of five people in a small town, run by Mr Desmond Hale, who's 66. I'm engaged to Luis, a carpenter, and we're saving for a church wedding next autumn, though honestly we've got less than a month of money put by. We rent a small house two streets from my parents.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I prepare accounts and tax returns for family businesses, farmers, the parish church and a few retired people with rental cottages. Most of it is paper: clients bring in folders, I enter it all, reconcile the bank and draft the accounts for Mr Hale to check. I like the clients, I've known half of them since Sunday school, and I like getting the numbers right. What wears me out is that I'm still slow and I make small mistakes, and Mr Hale writes 'see me' in pencil on my files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, because I never trusted those computer programs to understand people's affairs. At work I'd tell Mr Hale we were right not to waste money on it. I'm not online much, but I'd tell my mum and the ladies at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still worry, because the worry was never really about AI. Mr Hale is 66 and he's talked about selling the firm, and if a big firm from the city buys us, they'll bring their own systems and their own people. With few firms round here, a wedding to pay for and almost no savings, I don't feel settled at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder on my accuracy so Mr Hale has fewer 'see me' notes, because if he sells, I want a good reference. I'd ask him straight whether he's planning to retire in the next two years. And Luis and I would cut back the wedding, maybe the church hall instead of the hotel, to save around £3,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. AI Plateau doesn't fix my boss Mr Hale getting older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean for you if Mr Hale sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm from the city would probably keep the clients and close the office here, or keep one person. I'd be the junior with the slowest work. I might have to drive forty minutes each way, if they even kept me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did it feel to cut the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stung a bit, my mum had her heart set on the hotel. But my dad said a wedding is one day and a marriage is the rest of it. The church hall is where we had my nan's ninetieth anyway.

say: I'd say I'm glad; I never trusted **computer programs** with people's affairs.
I'd tell Mr Hale we were right not to **waste money** on it.
think: My worry was never AI; it's Mr Hale's **age** and a possible **sale**.
A city firm would bring its **own systems** and people.
do: Improve my **accuracy** so I earn a good reference.
Ask Mr Hale whether he'll **retire** within two years.
Move the wedding to the **church hall**, saving about £3,000.
feel: **Anxious**; the plateau doesn't fix my boss **getting older**.
S0.quote: AI Plateau doesn't fix my boss Mr Hale getting older.
fieldNote: Her main risk is **succession**, not technology: a 66-year-old owner.
Would **shrink the wedding** rather than borrow, a traditional thrift instinct.
Distrusts AI out of **values**, not experience.

steps.text: Keep preparing church and farm accounts more carefully at Hale & Co
Cut the wedding budget by about £3,000
Move the reception from the hotel to the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because accounting is about trust and knowing your clients, and a computer can't do that. At work I'd say we should keep doing things properly. With friends I'd say every generation has had changes, and we'll get through it with hard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm frightened it means the end of a firm like ours. If the big firms can do returns with software at half our price, Mr Hale's clients will drift away, or he'll sell sooner. And I don't use these tools at all, so I'd be the first to go anywhere that did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams, even though they're hard, because a qualification is worth something anywhere. I'd ask Mr Hale whether the church and the farmers would stay with us if we kept doing it the old way, with a face they know. And I'd ask Luis about doing the books for his carpentry, so at least some work stays in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like the ground's going soft under me and I can't see where it's firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new software if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, but I'd hate every minute. I learned on paper ledgers from my boss, and I trust what I can tick with a pencil. I'd want someone patient to show me, not a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the government, really; I'd rather people stood on their own feet. Families, churches, employers who've had good years from their staff. The big firms using this software should be training people, not dropping them.

say: Accounting is about **trust** and knowing your clients.
We'll get through it with **hard work**, like every generation.
think: It may mean **the end** of a small firm like ours.
I don't use AI, so I'd be **first to go** anywhere that did.
do: Finish my **exams** for a qualification that's worth something anywhere.
Ask Mr Hale if clients would stay for **a face they know**.
Do the **books for Luis's** carpentry to keep work in the family.
S1.quote: I learned on paper ledgers from my boss, and I trust what I can tick with a pencil.
fieldNote: Fears **cheap software** will pull clients away from a small family firm.
Prefers **family, church and employers** over government help.
Would learn tools only **reluctantly**, wanting a patient person to teach her.

steps.text: Pass the remaining accountancy exams this year
Keep serving church and farm clients face to face at Hale & Co
Keep the books for Luis's carpentry work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's arrived too fast and people should look after their own, their families and neighbours. At work I'd say we'll keep the doors open as long as clients want us. At church I'd pray about it, I'm not embarrassed to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's finished by 2029. It's all thinking work, the numbers and the forms, and the AI does that from 2028. Luis is different, his work is hands-on. My fiancé Luis is a carpenter, so he's got until about 2031 before robots can fit a staircase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd postpone the wedding, or make it the smallest service possible, and put every pound into savings. I'd ask Luis to take me on as his helper, doing his paperwork and learning to sand and finish, because his work lasts three years longer. And once it arrived, I'd lean on my parents, maybe move into their spare room to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel sick, but I'd have Luis and my family, which is more than some people have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luis the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's your turn to keep us. He'd laugh and then he'd go quiet. Then we'd sit down with a pencil and work out whether we could still afford the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'look after their own'. Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was nothing else, yes, I wouldn't let us go hungry out of pride. But I'd go to my family first. That's how my parents did it when the factory closed.

say: It's **too fast**; people should look after **their own**.
We'll keep the **doors open** as long as clients want us.
think: My job's **finished by 2029**; it's all thinking work.
Luis's carpentry lasts to **about 2031**, before robots can fit staircases.
do: **Postpone** or shrink the wedding and save every pound.
Become **Luis's helper**, doing paperwork and finishing work.
Lean on **my parents**, maybe moving into their spare room.
feel: **Alarmed** and sick, but I have **Luis and family**.
S2.quote: My fiancé Luis is a carpenter, so he's got until about 2031 before robots can fit a staircase.
fieldNote: Grasps the **robot gap**: her desk work goes in 2028, her fiancé's trade later.
Family is her **first safety net**; state help only as a last resort.
Not panicked because she has **people to lean on**, despite no savings.

steps.text: Postpone the church wedding or hold the smallest service possible
Put every spare pound into a joint savings account
Work as Luis's helper doing paperwork and finishing
Move into her parents' spare room to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and sensible people would start preparing. At work I'd tell Mr Hale it might be the right time to sell, while the firm's still worth something. At church I'd say we should help the young ones learn trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to get married and maybe qualify, but my job still ends by 2031. What matters is I'd have time to learn something with my hands before the robots around 2034. And Luis could build up his business a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, we'd have the wedding, but small, and I'd finish the exams. Then I'd go part-time at Hale & Co and help Luis properly, learning to finish furniture and handle his customers. We'd save £100 a month toward his workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but I'd feel like we had a plan. It's hard, but it's honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Hale did sell in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask the buyer to keep me for a year to hand over the clients, since I know them all. After that, I'd go full-time with Luis. I'd rather work with my hands for family than at a desk for strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for Luis's quotes and invoices, if it saved time. I'd still check every line. I'm not changing who I am.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning**, and sensible people would start preparing.
The church should help **young people learn trades**.
think: I can marry and **qualify**, but my job ends by 2031.
There's time to learn **hands-on work** before robots around 2034.
do: Hold a **small wedding** and finish my exams.
Go **part-time** and help Luis finish furniture.
Save **£100 a month** toward his workshop.
feel: **Alarmed**, but we'd have **a plan** of honest work.
S3.quote: I'd rather work with my hands for family than at a desk for strangers.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose her accounting job** by 2031.
Five years lets her **join her fiancé's trade** before robots arrive.
Would ask a buyer to keep her for a **handover year**.

steps.text: Hold a small church wedding in the first year
Pass the remaining exams before leaving accounting
Go part-time and learn furniture finishing with Luis
Save £100 a month toward Luis's workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time enough for people to do the right thing. At work I'd say Mr Hale should plan his retirement and the firm's future properly. At church I'd say pray, then plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough for us to marry, maybe start a family, and build Luis's business. My accounting job still goes in 2036, but I'd have a decade of doing his books, and maybe others in town. I'd be 37 and settled, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, wedding and exams. Then I'd build a little bookkeeping service for local tradespeople alongside Hale & Co, and by the early 2030s I'd be working with Luis full-time. We'd save toward buying a house, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but further away. Ten years of warning makes AGI a cloud on the horizon, not over our heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want them in the first few years of marriage anyway. Ten years means they'd be at school when it hits. That worries me more than my own job, what work they'll do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands, and to be good with people. And to go to church and know their neighbours. Those things don't go out of date.

say: I'd say ten years is **time enough** for people to do the right thing.
Mr Hale should plan his **retirement** properly.
think: Ten years is enough to **marry**, start a family and build Luis's business.
My job still goes in 2036, but I'd have **a decade** of local books.
do: Have the **wedding** and finish exams in year one.
Build a **bookkeeping service** for local tradespeople.
Work with **Luis full-time** by the early 2030s.
feel: **Anxious** but distant; a **cloud** on the horizon.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning makes AGI a cloud on the horizon, not over our heads.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **plan a family** and a move into her fiancé's trade.
Worries more for **future children** than for herself.
Values **hands, people and faith** as things that don't date.

steps.text: Marry Luis and plan for children early in the marriage
Offer bookkeeping to local tradespeople alongside her firm job
Join Luis's carpentry business full-time by the early 2030s
Save slowly toward buying a house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time to learn anything new and we've no savings. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, and businesses keeping people on to train them. Family will help us, but they can't pay our rent forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people round here would get through this with their church and their families. Nobody can automate a church hall full of people bringing casseroles.

headlineQuote: Nobody can automate a church hall full of people bringing casseroles.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old **junior** at a five-person **family firm** whose owner is 66.
Engaged to Luis, a **carpenter**, she has under a month saved and a wedding to fund.
Traditional and wary of tech, she **never uses AI** and leans on family and church.
She's anxious even in the plateau, **alarmed** in faster scenarios, and plans to join **Luis's trade**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to learn and no **savings**.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for adults and employers who **train** staff.
